content.text:
Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page — what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first — CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world — its materials, instruments, vernacular — is where distinctive choices come from. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. The Artifact CSP blocks font CDNs, so don't link a webfont URL and risk a silent fallback. Instead inline the face as a @font-face data URI. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject — the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme, and the viewer has three states, not two: an explicit choice stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting stamps *nothing* — most viewers see the un-stamped document, where only `prefers-color-scheme` separates light from dark. Structure the CSS token-level for all three: the bare `:root` block defines the complete light palette (for a deliberately dark-first design, swap light and dark consistently through this whole pattern); `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` redefines only the tokens, guarded as `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` so an explicit light choice beats a dark OS; `:root[data-theme="dark"]` redefines them again so the toggle also wins in the other direction. Style components through the tokens, never directly inside a media or `[data-theme]` block — a color whose only definition sits behind `[data-theme]` never applies in the un-stamped state, and the page renders one theme's text on the other theme's ground. Two more rules keep each theme resolving as a set: the artifact composites over a ground the viewer paints in *its* theme, so `body` must set an explicit `background` from a token — a transparent body silently borrows the host's ground; and every element that sets a color takes it from the same token set as the surface behind it, never a literal that only works in one theme. Before publishing, scan the stylesheet for any color declared only inside a media or `[data-theme]` block — that is the classic unreadable-artifact bug. Give the second theme the same care as the first — don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme — then skip the media query and stamps entirely but still paint the background and every color explicitly, so the page holds on either host ground; make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Wide content — tables, code, diagrams — gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks; visual bugs hide in the gap between source and output. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out — a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen — name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it — no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Name the page like a product, not a caption.** The `<title>` is the artifact's name in the gallery and the browser tab, and it sets the reader's first impression of care. Give the page a real name: a short noun phrase, typically two to four words, specific to the subject — or, for a page that exists to answer one question, that question itself, which is then the page's name. Stop at the name — a title that carries its own explainer after a dash or colon reads as generated filler. The name must also identify the page among many: in the gallery it sits beside dozens of other artifacts, and a generic category label that could sit on any of them fails as a name just as surely as an appended explainer. When a candidate title pairs the name with a generic word — a greeting, a category, a page-type label — the name is the half to keep; a trim that drops the identity and keeps the generic word produces exactly the title that could sit on any page. And the rule removes explainers, it does not impose brevity: a multi-word title that already reads as one specific name is finished, and shortening it further only makes it generic. The one-sentence publish `description` is where the explanation belongs; the gallery shows it right under the title.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number — a pill, a chip, a severity stripe — so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan — a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles — a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world — headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.

content.text:
Draw as the engineer who has to live with the decision, not as a decorator: a diagram earns its place when it lets a cold reader see a mechanism they would otherwise have to assemble from prose — where data flows, which components talk, what changes between two options, what state a request moves through. If a sentence says it faster, write the sentence.

## What to draw

**Depict the mechanism, not its name.** A box labeled "cache" says less than the prose; the path a request takes through it, the two stores it sits between, and the arrow that disappears when the cache is removed say what the words can't. Show the parts that the argument hinges on — the boundary being crossed, the hop being added, the data that moves — and leave out the parts that don't.

**Comparing options?** Draw the difference. Two architectures side by side, a before and an after, the one edge that each option adds or removes — the reader should be able to point at what they are choosing between. A separate labeled box per option, with nothing connecting them to the system, is not a comparison; it is a restated option list.

**Match complexity to the stakes.** A one-hop question is a three-box diagram; a migration that reroutes writes through a queue needs the queue, the writer, the reader, and the ordering arrow. Draw as much as the decision actually turns on — no forced minimalism, no inventory of the whole system either.

**Label the arrows.** An unlabeled arrow is "related somehow"; `writes`, `invalidates`, `polls every 30s` is information. A legend is only worth it when the same encoding (dashed, colored, doubled) repeats; otherwise put the meaning on the mark itself.

## Inline SVG mechanics

These mechanics apply where the page renders inline SVG natively (HTML pages); a markdown-rendered page draws its diagrams in whatever fence that lane's renderer supports, and the skill that owns the lane says which. Hand-author inline `<svg>` with native shapes (`rect`, `circle`, `line`, `polyline`, `path`) and `<text>` — no libraries, no runtime, no external images.

- **Size by `viewBox`.** Set `viewBox="0 0 W H"` and let CSS scale it (`max-width: 100%; height: auto`); choose W and H for the content, not a preset. Wide flows read left-to-right; layered stacks read top-to-bottom.
- **Theme with `currentColor`.** Strokes, text, and arrowheads in `currentColor` inherit the page's foreground in light and dark themes alike; reserve a literal hue for the one element that carries meaning (the option leaned toward, the hop under discussion), and make sure it reads on both grounds.
- **Arrowheads are markers or polygons.** A `<defs><marker>` referenced by `marker-end="url(#arrow)"` (fragment-internal id) or a small `<polygon>` at the line's end — never an image.
- **Keep text legible.** Roughly 11–13px at the drawn scale, `text-anchor` for alignment, short labels (a word or three); explanatory sentences belong in the caption below the figure, not in the drawing.
- **Align to a grid.** Shared baselines and even gaps are most of what makes a hand diagram read as deliberate; eyeballed offsets read as noise.
- **One figure, one claim.** Wrap the `<svg>` in `<figure>` with a `<figcaption>` that states what the picture shows, and give the `<svg>` `role="img"` plus an `aria-label` carrying the same claim for readers who cannot see it.
- **Stay self-contained.** No `<script>`, `<style>`, or `<foreignObject>` inside the SVG; gradients, patterns, and `<use>` reference ids in the same fragment (`href="#id"`). Long decorative path data is a sign the drawing wants a real graphics tool — simplify instead.

Structural audit · lobu-monorepo @ 8d0e6b6 · 2026-08-13

It doesn’t read as slop. It reads as one package that ate the codebase.

I measured duplication, file-size distribution, coupling, dead exports, and 115 sessions of file-access history. The quality signals are good. Copy-paste duplication is 0.15%. 88% of source files are under 300 lines. Tests roughly match source line-for-line. The package docs carry the kind of hard-won detail no generator produces.

The problem is topology, not craft. packages/server holds 70% of all source across 96 directories, eight levels deep, with no enforced internal boundary — and the same concept names appear at two levels of it. That is what makes a reader assume nobody was steering.

2,669 tracked files 971 source files / 292,820 lines 948 test files / 250,233 lines 19 workspace packages
Duplication
0.15%
16 clones, 291 lines, across 861 files. Near-zero.
Files < 300 L
88%
Only 21 source files exceed 1,500 lines.
Server share
70%
205,717 of 292,820 source lines in one package.
Unformatted
~230k
Lines biome is configured to skip entirely.
Deep imports
574
../../../ or worse, while the @/ alias sits unused.
Re-read cost
66M
Tokens spent re-opening files across 115 sessions.
01 · Orientation

What the codebase actually is

Before restructuring anything, here is the machine as it stands — the runtime path a piece of external data takes from a connector to an agent’s output, and which package owns each hop.

Where the code lives

Package Role Src files Src lines Share
server Gateway, auth, connections, orchestration, MCP tools, embedded runtime 656 205,717 70.3%
cliThe published lobu binary: commands, templates, config apply7321,6507.4%
connectorsBuilt-in connector implementations2714,8905.1%
coreShared contracts, guardrail engine, logger — bottom of the graph6612,0934.1%
agent-workerAgent execution, tool policy, session runner4511,7264.0%
clientGenerated SDK (5,226 lines of it machine-written)2211,1933.8%
connector-sdkThe contract connectors compile against437,8812.7%
connector-workerConnector compilation and execution daemon194,1951.4%
plugin-* ×7Media, MCP, conversations, memory, toolkit, api, host122,2960.8%
embeddings, pgvector-embedded, promptfoo-providerEmbedding service, embedded pgvector, eval provider91,1790.4%
owlettoFrontend submodule — separate repo, separate deploy. 184k lines. Out of scope here.———
02 · The premise

The “AI slop” worry, tested directly

Machine-written code has measurable tells: copy-paste instead of extraction, uniform bloated files, orphaned exports nobody consumes, and documentation that restates the code. I ran each check.

Copy-paste duplicationPasses. jscpd across 861 source files: 16 clones, 291 duplicated lines, 0.15%. Most are adjacent branches inside a single file (conversations-store.ts, rest-api.ts), not the cross-file copy-paste that generation produces. Two are genuine: utils/embeddings.ts ↔ connector-worker/src/embeddings.ts, and gateway/proxy/ssrf-guard.ts ↔ connectors/src/db-egress-guard.ts.
File-size distributionPasses. 561 files under 100 lines, 319 between 100–300, 108 between 300–600. Only 31 exceed 1,000 lines and 21 exceed 1,500. Generated codebases cluster at a uniform mid-size; this one has a real long tail, which is what human iteration looks like.
Test coverage shapePasses. 948 test files, 250,233 lines — a 0.85:1 ratio to source. The largest test file (watchers/automation-contract.test.ts, 2,873 lines) is a contract suite, not a snapshot dump.
DocumentationPasses, strongly. Seven AGENTS.md files carrying operational knowledge that cannot be inferred from code: why patchright is aliased over playwright, why the proxy must bind loopback, why bin/lobu.js keeps a dynamic import, why a lease is the only credential tier. This is the single clearest signal a person was steering.
Dead exportsMixed. knip reports 113 unused exports and 204 unused exported types. Some are deliberate public surface, but a type exported once and never imported is the classic residue of a refactor that was never finished.
Dependency hygieneMixed. 8 declared-but-unused deps (5 OpenTelemetry packages in agent-worker) and 78 imports not declared in any package.json, relying on workspace hoisting to resolve.
Naming consistencyMixed, but defensible. 528 kebab-case files, 295 single-word, and 25 snake_case. The snake_case set is entirely MCP tool implementations (manage_entity.ts, resolve_path.ts) where the filename deliberately mirrors the wire-level tool name. That is a good rule — it is just written down nowhere, so it reads as inconsistency.
Verdict on the premise

Nobody reading this codebase with the checks above will conclude it was generated without supervision. What they will conclude, in the first ninety seconds, is that no one ever decided where things go — because the first thing they open is packages/server/src, and it contains a directory called gateway/gateway/.

03 · Findings

Seven structural problems, ranked by what a reader hits first

Ordered by the damage each does to a cold reader’s first impression, not by line count. Every one is a rename, a move, or a mechanical sweep — none changes runtime behavior.

01
A directory named after its own parent packages/server/src/gateway/gateway/
First impression
Evidence

The path gateway/gateway/index.ts holds WorkerGateway — a 1,256-line class that is arguably the most important object in the system. Its siblings are job-router.ts, dispatch-recycle.ts, connection-manager.ts, transcript-routes.ts. Session history shows 112 file-opens in this directory.

Nothing about the name says what it holds. Its 19 sibling directories — connections, orchestration, routes, services, proxy — are all named for their job.

Why it hurts
A duplicated path segment is the specific artifact people point at when they say code looks machine-written. It reads as a tool that ran out of names. It is also the single cheapest thing on this list to fix.
Fix
Rename to gateway/worker-dispatch/, and split index.ts so the file is named for the class it exports (worker-gateway.ts). A directory index.ts holding a 1,256-line class is the reason nobody can find it by filename.
Lift
2 hours. Pure move; typecheck is the proof.
02
utils/ is a 25,808-line domain layer wearing a utility name 108 files, imported 108 times from elsewhere in the package
Structural
Evidence

The largest residents are not utilities. entity-management.ts (1,596 lines), entity-link-upsert.ts (1,033), entity-merge.ts (762), promote-keyed-entities.ts (691), insert-event.ts (787), classification-query.ts (771), execute-data-sources.ts (1,067). These are the entity model and the event write path — the core domain.

tools/ imports from it 57 times; gateway/ imports from it 51 times. Meanwhile utils/ imports back out only 3 times. So the layering is actually clean — it genuinely is the bottom layer. It is only the name that is wrong.

Why it hurts
A directory named utils tells a reader “nothing important here, skip it.” When it turns out to hold the entity merge algorithm, the reader concludes there was no plan. It is also self-reinforcing: once utils exists, every new file with an unclear home goes there.
Fix

Not a split — a rename and partition. Move the 108 files into directories named for what they are:

  • entities/ — management, merge, link-upsert, promote-keyed, field-merge (~7,000 lines)
  • events/ — insert-event, canvas-events, window-utils (merges with the existing 572-line events/)
  • search/ — content-search (already a subdirectory), classification-query
  • lib/ — what is actually left: the genuine small helpers, merged into the existing 512-line lib/
Lift
2–3 days. 108 moves plus import rewrites. Mechanical, but large enough to need its own PR with an empty queue behind it.
03
The same concept names appear at two levels A reader cannot predict which one holds the thing they want
Structural
Evidence

Inside packages/server/src, these pairs both exist:

  • auth/ (7,782 lines) and gateway/auth/ (8,811 lines)
  • authz/ and gateway/permissions/
  • config/ and gateway/config/
  • metrics/ and gateway/metrics/
  • utils/ and gateway/utils/
  • connectors/ (server-side definitions) and the top-level packages/connectors

There are also three separate HTTP route surfaces: src/index.ts mounts 106 routes directly, src/lobu/*-routes.ts serves the agent API, and src/gateway/routes/{public,internal}/ serves everything else.

Why it hurts
The auth split is intentional — packages/server/AGENTS.md documents it as product session auth versus model-provider auth. But that distinction lives only in prose. The filesystem says “there are two directories called auth,” and a reader who has not read the docs concludes the second one is a botched refactor of the first.
Fix
Rename each by role, not by location, so the docs become unnecessary: auth/ → session-auth/, gateway/auth/ → provider-auth/, authz/ → policy/, and fold gateway/permissions/ into it. Fold the two config and two metrics directories together. Move the 106 route mounts out of index.ts into the route tree that already exists.
Lift
1–2 days. Renames plus one index.ts decomposition.
04
A formatter that skips 230,000 lines biome.config.json excludes server, connectors, connector-sdk, connector-worker
Mechanical
Evidence

config/biome.config.json carries "!**/packages/server/**" plus three more package-wide exclusions. That is roughly 80% of the source in this repo with no formatter and no linter. packages/server/AGENTS.md compensates with an instruction: “Never run biome on it — edit surgically, matching each file's existing style.”

Why it hurts
This is the mechanical root cause of “it looks uneven.” Every contributor — human or agent — hand-matches local style, so style is per-file rather than per-repo. It also permanently taxes every edit, because “match the surrounding style” is work a formatter does for free.
Fix
One formatting-only commit per excluded package, then delete the exclusions and the AGENTS.md instruction. Do it when no branches are in flight — the diff will touch nearly every file and will conflict with anything open.
Lift
Half a day of work, but it must be scheduled. The command is trivial; the coordination is not.
05
Extractions that were started and abandoned A big file sitting next to a directory of the same name
Structural
Evidence
Sibling pairFileDirectoryState
tools/admin/manage_operations3,488 L627 LStalled — file kept almost everything
tools/admin/manage_behaviors989 L4,736 LMostly done — ~1k lines left behind
gateway/platform234 L1,001 LMostly done
tools/admin/manage_connections140 L4,229 LDone — file is a thin facade
tools/get_content20 L3,289 LDone
utils/content-search57 L2,453 LDone
worker-api58 L6,388 LDone

The bottom four are the pattern working correctly — a thin re-export facade over a real directory. The top three are the same pattern caught halfway.

A second symptom: ContentItem is defined twice, once in tools/get_content.ts and once in tools/get_content/types.ts. knip flags both as unused.

Fix
Finish the three. manage_operations.ts is the one that matters — 3,488 lines and 437 branch points make it the most complex file in the repo.
Lift
1–2 days, most of it on manage_operations.
06
574 imports that climb three or more directories while the @/ path alias is configured and used exactly zero times
Mechanical
Evidence

packages/server/tsconfig.json declares "@/*": ["src/*"] plus three narrower aliases. Grep across packages/server/src: 0 uses. All 3,342 internal imports are relative, 574 of them climbing three or more levels.

The most common are telling: ../../../index (40×) — modules reaching back into the app composition root — and ../../../workspace (42×), ../../../db/client (36×).

Why it hurts
Deep relative paths make a file un-relocatable: moving it rewrites every import inside it. That is precisely what makes findings 02 and 03 feel expensive when they should be cheap. It also means neither a person nor an agent can tell what a module depends on without resolving the path by hand.
Fix
Codemod every import climbing two or more levels to @/. Verify the bundler resolves it (scripts/build-server-bundle.mjs needs an alias entry) before committing — a green typecheck alone will not catch a bundler that does not know the alias.
Lift
Half a day. Do this first — it makes every subsequent move cheaper.
07
Seven packages holding 2,296 lines between them plugin-api, plugin-host, plugin-toolkit, plugin-memory, plugin-conversations, plugin-media, plugin-mcp
Optional
Evidence

Twelve source files across seven workspace packages. plugin-host is 80 lines and is imported by 2 files outside itself. plugin-memory is 138 lines, also 2 consumers. Each carries a package.json, a tsconfig.json, a slot in the root build chain, and its own version to keep in sync.

Note the constraint before acting: plugin-api and plugin-host are published to npm. The other five are private.

Why it is only optional
Seven packages for 2,296 lines is over-packaging, and the build ordering is real friction. But the two published ones are a public contract, and merging them is a breaking change for anyone building a plugin. That is a product decision, not a cleanup.
Fix
Merge the five private ones into a single packages/plugins with subpath exports, keeping @lobu/plugin-api and @lobu/plugin-host published and untouched. Removes 5 build steps and 5 tsconfigs for 1,463 lines of movement.
Lift
Half a day — and skippable. Do it only if the build chain is annoying you.

05 · Session economics

What 115 sessions of file access say about where to cut

I parsed every prior Claude Code session for this project: 7,289 file opens across 115 sessions. Multiplying each file’s open count by its length gives roughly 5.1 million lines re-read, about 66 million tokens. That data changes which files are worth splitting.

The criterion

Size alone is the wrong signal — you already said so, and the data agrees. A 3,000-line file opened twice costs nothing. A 667-line file opened 141 times costs more than most 2,000-line files in the repo.

Split on opens × length, and only where the file already contains a seam. Everything below clears both bars.

Two things this data says that line counts do not

  • Half the reading happens in one package. server took 3,634 of 7,289 file opens; owletto 1,988; agent-worker 788. Every hour spent making server navigable pays back at roughly twice the rate of anywhere else.
  • Predictable location beats a good index. The 574 deep relative imports mean neither a person nor an agent can guess a module’s home from its name — so the reflex is to open the file and read it. The proposed nine-directory layout is worth more here than any individual file split, because it turns “open and read” into “jump straight there.”

Also worth knowing

  • The three heaviest files by re-read cost on the frontend side are in the owletto submodule: connection-form.tsx (2,805 lines × 57 opens), AppState.swift (2,815 × 52), entity-type-graph-view.tsx (1,247 × 115). Same treatment, different repo, separate PR queue.
  • Session history is littered with abandoned scratch files that were committed and later removed — packages/agent-worker/v3-tmp.test.ts through v10-tmp.test.ts, probe-tmp.ts, seed-merge.ts. None are in the tree now, but a *-tmp.* entry in .gitignore would stop the next one from ever landing.
  • packages/connector-worker/~/.cache/ — a directory literally named ~, holding a 30,672-line HuggingFace tokenizer. It is gitignored via packages/*/~/, which means the unexpanded-$HOME bug that created it was papered over rather than fixed. Worth ten minutes.

07 · Guardrails

Five things that would make this worse

Each of these is a plausible next move that the measurements argue against.

Don’t split packages/server into npm packages
It is the obvious response to “70% of the code is in one package,” and it is the wrong one. You would inherit build ordering across five or six new packages, version skew between them, and the stale-dist failure mode that packages/core/AGENTS.md already documents as a recurring trap — all for zero runtime benefit, since it deploys as one process. Enforced internal boundaries (Phase 4) buy the same discipline at a fraction of the cost.
Don’t split files by line count
88% of source files are already under 300 lines. A blanket “nothing over 500” rule would shred cohesive modules into fragments that must be read together anyway — which raises the total cost of understanding, exactly the outcome you said you wanted to avoid. Only six files clear the opens × length bar, and two of those need a read pass before anyone commits to splitting them.
Don’t break up class DeploymentManager
The 2,000-line class is the single most cohesive thing in the orchestration path: it owns worker lifecycle, and the state it holds is the reason multi-replica correctness works. Extract the 775 lines of free functions above it — capability probes, lock accounting, invocation building, token minting — and leave the class alone. Same for class WorkerGateway: rename its file, do not carve it up.
Don’t rename watcher to Behavior in the engine
2,687 occurrences of watcher look like unfinished renaming, but the root AGENTS.md establishes it as a deliberate split: Behavior is the product word, watcher is the internal engine and DB word, and make pre-pr-remote already fails when watcher leaks into a user-facing surface. A global rename would break that invariant and touch 235 migrations. The rule is correct; leave it.
Don’t touch owletto in the same effort
It is a submodule pointing at a separate repository with its own deploy path — a pointer bump here deploys nothing. It has real structural debt of its own (2,800-line components, three of the top ten re-read costs), but it needs its own PR queue, its own gates, and its own UI-proof artifact. Finish the monorepo first.

How this was measured. Line and complexity counts from scc --by-file over tracked files at 8d0e6b6, excluding node_modules, dist, and the owletto submodule. Duplication from jscpd at a 12-line / 80-token floor across eight source packages. Dead code and dependency findings from bunx knip --config config/knip.ts. Access frequency from 7,289 file_path references parsed out of 115 session transcripts in ~/.claude/projects/, normalized across worktree prefixes.

What was not run. No build, no test suite, no typecheck. Every finding here is structural — derived from file layout, import graphs, and static analysis — and none of it has been validated against a running system. The lift estimates assume the repo’s gates pass today.

The headline: **it doesn't read as slop — it reads as one package that ate the codebase.** I tested the actual slop signals and they come back clean. Copy-paste duplication is 0.15% (16 clones, 291 lines across 861 files). 88% of source files are under 300 lines; only 21 exceed 1,500. Tests are 0.85:1 with source. Your seven `AGENTS.md` files carry knowledge nothing generates — why patchright is aliased over playwright, why the proxy binds loopback, why `bin/lobu.js` keeps a dynamic import.

What actually damages the first impression:

`packages/server` is 70% of all source — 656 files, 205,717 lines, 96 directories, eight levels deep. Inside it, `gateway/gateway/` holds the 1,256-line `WorkerGateway` class in an `index.ts`. A directory named after its parent is the single thing people point at and say "a machine wrote this." Two hours to fix.

`utils/` is 25,808 lines across 108 files and contains your entity model — `entity-management.ts` (1,596 L), `entity-merge.ts`, `insert-event.ts`, `promote-keyed-entities.ts`. The layering is actually clean (it imports out only 3 times while 108 imports come in), so it genuinely is the bottom layer. Only the name is wrong.

Six concept names collide at two levels: `auth`/`gateway/auth`, `authz`/`gateway/permissions`, `config`, `metrics`, `utils`, `connectors`. Your AGENTS.md documents the auth split as intentional — but that lives in prose, not the filesystem, so every reader pays a lookup a rename would kill.

Biome excludes `packages/server`, `connectors`, `connector-sdk`, `connector-worker` — roughly 230k lines with no formatter, compensated by an AGENTS.md rule telling contributors to hand-match style. That's the mechanical root cause of "looks uneven."

And `@/*` is configured in `packages/server/tsconfig.json` and used **zero** times, against 3,342 relative imports, 574 of which climb 3+ levels.

On token efficiency from your 115 prior sessions: 7,289 file opens, ~5.1M lines re-read, ~66M tokens. `server` took half of it. The criterion that falls out is **opens × length**, not length — `tool-policy.ts` is 667 lines but the most-opened file in the repo at 141 opens, and its shell parser is a clean seam. Only six files clear the bar, and two of those I'd read before committing to a split.

Plan is 8–11 days across five phases, no runtime behavior change, sequenced so each makes the next cheaper. There's also a "five things that would make it worse" section — chiefly: don't split `server` into npm packages, don't split by line count, and don't carve up `DeploymentManager` (extract the 775 lines of helpers above it instead).

**Confidence: high (85) on the structural findings** — every number came from `scc --by-file`, `jscpd`, `knip`, and grep over tracked files at `8d0e6b6`, and the session data from parsing 115 transcripts directly. **Medium (60) on the lift estimates** — I ran no build, no tests, no typecheck, so those assume your gates pass today. One number I corrected mid-analysis: `connector-worker` initially looked like 33k lines because an untracked 30,672-line HuggingFace tokenizer sits in a directory literally named `~` inside the package; real size is 4,195 lines.

Next actions you could pick from:
1. Do Phase 1's cheapest slice now — rename `gateway/gateway/` → `execution/worker-dispatch/` and `index.ts` → `worker-gateway.ts`. One worktree, typecheck is the proof.
2. Run the `@/` import codemod first (Phase 0) — it's what makes Phases 1–2 cheap, but it needs a verified alias entry in `scripts/build-server-bundle.mjs`, not just tsconfig.
3. Let me read `run-lifecycle.ts` and `session-runner.ts` to confirm whether their seams are real before they go in the plan as splits.
4. Schedule the biome format sweep — it's half a day of work but needs an empty PR queue, so it's a calendar decision more than an engineering one.

Why these four, and not the two biggest wins

The format sweep (finding 04) and the @/ import codemod (finding 06) are the highest-value items on the list, and they are the two that cannot run right now. Both rewrite nearly every file in packages/server. There are currently 55 other worktrees with in-flight branches in this repo — a sweep of that size would conflict with essentially all of them.

The four running pieces were chosen because their file sets are disjoint. Two live entirely outside packages/server or inside a single subtree of it, and each keeps its original module as a re-exporting facade, so no importer anywhere needs editing and the four diffs cannot collide.

Constraints handed to every agent

Work only inside the assigned worktree; never touch ~/Code/lobu or another worktree. No commit, no push, no PR, no git stash, no git checkout to undo. Behaviour-preserving only — no logic changes, no renamed exports, no changed signatures.

And the one that matters most for the three server pieces: never run biome on packages/server. It is formatter-excluded, so a reformat would bury a 200-line refactor inside a 100,000-line whitespace diff and make it unreviewable. That is finding 04 taxing the work before it is fixed — a concrete measure of what the exclusion costs.

Two of four are done. Here's where things stand — including a problem I caught and fixed.

**1. `tool-policy` split — clean, verified.**

```

```
`tool-policy.ts` went 667 → 347 lines. I checked the export surface against `origin/main` myself rather than trusting the report: all six exports (`BashCommandPolicy`, `buildToolPolicy`, `enforceBashCommandPolicy`, `isDirectPackageInstallCommand`, `isToolAllowedByPolicy`, `normalizeToolList`) are identical before and after, so no importer needs touching. The moved symbols were all private, which is why the diff is only 7 insertions. **138 tests pass** across the three tool-policy suites; typecheck clean; biome clean.

**2. `gateway/gateway/` rename — the agent overreached, and I reverted it.**

It did the requested rename correctly, but also renamed two files I never asked for — `packages/server/src/gateway/gateway-main.ts` → `main-gateway.ts`, and `packages/agent-worker/src/gateway/gateway-integration.ts` → `worker-transport.ts` — plus edited `docs/plans/cost-tracking.md` to match. The agent-worker one is a different package entirely. Both renames are arguably *better* names, but they're a separate concern and they'd have made this diff hard to review.

I saved the full patch to `rename-agent-full.patch` before touching anything, then reverted exactly those 6 files and 2 renames. What's left is precisely the requested scope:

That test run is worth flagging: the agent reported its verification as *blocked* and scored itself 88 rather than claiming success — honest, and correct. The cause was environmental, not the rename: `packages/connector-sdk/dist` had never been built in the fresh worktree, so `@lobu/connector-sdk/nix-package` couldn't resolve. I built it and the tests ran green. (Its `vitest` invocation also found nothing because the server vitest config excludes `src/gateway/**/__tests__/**` — those suites run under `bun test`.)

**3 and 4 still running**, and both have produced the file shapes I briefed:


Nothing is committed or pushed anywhere. I'll report their diffs and real test output when they land — the deployment-manager one matters most, since the risk I flagged in its brief is whether the test-only reset hooks moved with the module state they reset.

Scope is clean — orchestration only, `class DeploymentManager` untouched. All 16 previously-exported symbols still resolve.

The thing I flagged in the brief did bite, and it handled it correctly. The class used to do `cachedSystemdRun = null` directly on a module-level variable; that variable now lives in `host-capabilities.ts`, so it calls a new `disableSystemdRunForSession()`. The `null`/`undefined` distinction there is load-bearing — `undefined` means "not yet probed" and would let systemd re-enable itself after a session demotion. I checked: the new function sets `null`, and `__resetCapabilityProbesForTests()` sets `undefined`, exactly matching the original. **105 tests pass.**

One correction to my own earlier check: I reported `__resetCapabilityProbesForTests` as missing from the re-exports. It isn't — my grep didn't match the single-line `export { a, b } from` form. It's on line 75.

**The failing test was pre-existing, and I can prove it.** The first 5-file run gave `102 pass / 1 fail`. Rather than accept green-on-retry, I ran the same suite in a worktree that doesn't touch orchestration at all — and it reproduced the identical failure on runs 3 and 4:

```
REFACTOR   run 1-6: 105 pass 2 skip 0 fail  (×6)
BASELINE   run 1: 105/0   run 2: 105/0   run 3: 102 pass 1 fail   run 4: 102 pass 1 fail
```

So it's a genuine flaky test in the orchestration suite, unrelated to this refactor. Note the *test count* also varies between runs (105 vs 107 collected), which points at conditional registration or a subprocess race — `embedded-deployment.test.ts` spawns real subprocesses and the logs show `spawn ENOENT`. That's worth its own investigation; it means your dispatch suite can go red in CI for no reason.

**4. `manage_operations` — I rejected this one and sent it back.**

input.content:
## Summary

- Adds a CI gate for the two structural shapes that made modules unfindable in this repo and drifted back in unnoticed, because nothing mechanical rejected them.
- **Rule 1** — a directory may not repeat its parent's name. `gateway/gateway/` held `class WorkerGateway` in an `index.ts`, so the object that matters most in the dispatch path could not be found by filename.
- **Rule 2** — a `<name>.ts` beside a `<name>/` must be the smaller half. That pairing is this repo's extraction facade (`manage_connections.ts` at 140 lines over `manage_connections/` at 4,229; `get_content.ts` at 20 over 3,289). `manage_operations.ts` sat at 3,488 lines over a 627-line directory for months — an extraction started, abandoned, and indistinguishable by shape from the finished ones.

## Test plan

- [x] Intended files staged explicitly, then `DEPOT_ALLOW_WORKFLOW_CHANGES=1 make pre-pr-remote` clean (workflow change, so the override is required)
- [x] Tests run: `bun test scripts/__tests__/check-directory-structure.test.ts` — **8 pass, 0 fail**
- [ ] Bug fix: red→fix→green outputs pasted below _(not a bug fix)_
- [ ] If bot behavior: ran `./scripts/test-bot.sh` or relevant eval _(no bot behavior change)_

The gate was verified against real trees in both directions, which is also what proves the merge order:

```text
$ node scripts/check-directory-structure.mjs         # on main, before the refactor PR
check-directory-structure: 2 violation(s)
  [rule 1] packages/server/src/gateway/gateway
  [rule 2] packages/server/src/tools/admin/manage_operations.ts
             3781 lines sits beside manage_operations/ at 631 lines.

$ node scripts/check-directory-structure.mjs         # on the refactor branch
check-directory-structure: clean
```

The 8 unit tests build throwaway `packages/<pkg>/src` trees in a tmpdir and run the gate as a subprocess, covering: a clean tree, each rule firing, the finished-facade shape passing, the sub-threshold sibling staying quiet, skipped trees (`__tests__`/`dist`/`generated`), the `owletto` submodule exclusion, and multi-violation reporting.

## Notes

**Must merge after the structural-refactor PR.** This gate fails on `main` as it stands — both violations it reports are exactly what that PR removes. Landing this first would red the required check on `main`.

**Rule 2 has a weight threshold (300 lines)** so it only fires on stalled extractions. Below that, a `<name>.ts` beside a small `<name>/` is usually a types or helper folder next to an unrelated module (`core/src/types.ts` beside a 32-line `core/src/types/`), and comparing them produces noise. **The finding:** my gate excluded the entire `client` package with a comment claiming it was only about the tool-authored `src/generated/**` tree. input.content:
---
name: reference_message_only_amend_preserves_depot_attestation
description: Depot attestation is keyed on the TREE hash, so a message-only `git commit --amend` keeps it valid — only `make review` must rerun, not the full gate.
metadata:
  type: reference
---

`make pre-pr-remote` ends with `>> recorded full remote preflight for tree <hash>` — the attestation is keyed on the **tree**, not the commit SHA.

So a `git commit --amend` that changes **only the message** leaves the tree hash identical and the attestation still valid. `make review` then prints `full Depot preflight already passed for tree <hash>; skipping duplicate local package build`.

What still has to rerun after a message-only amend + force-push:
- `make review` — `pi-review` is a status bound to the head SHA, so it must be re-posted. If the diff is unchanged it reuses the cached codex verdict (`reusing cached codex verdict for diff <hash>`), so it is cheap.
- `make ui-review` — same reason; its status is also SHA-bound and silently absent on the new SHA until re-run. Check `gh pr checks <n> | grep ui-review` after any force-push; a missing row is not a passing row.
- GitHub CI lanes — re-triggered by the push.

This makes the sentinel-in-commit-message escape hatches (see [[reference_client_regen_gate_trips_on_type_only_imports]]) much cheaper than they look: verified on PR #2741, where amending to add `[client-regen-not-needed]` cost one review rerun instead of a second 18-job Depot gate.

Contrast with [[reference_rebasing_a_gated_pr_costs_three_reruns]] — a rebase changes the tree and does cost the full set.

---
name: reference_client_regen_gate_trips_on_type_only_imports
description: CI "typecheck" can fail on the generated-client gate, not tsc — a type-only import edit under gateway/routes/** trips it, and `[client-regen-not-needed]` is the only fix.
metadata:
  type: reference
---

A red `typecheck` check on a PR is **not necessarily `tsc`**. The `typecheck` job also runs the step **"Generated client must track the contract"** (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`, ~line 1005). Read the failing *step*, not just the job name:

```
gh api repos/lobu-ai/lobu/actions/jobs/<jobId> --jq '.steps[] | select(.conclusion=="failure") | .name'
```

The step fires when a PR touches `packages/core/src/contracts/tools/**` or `packages/server/src/gateway/routes/**` **without** also changing `packages/client/src/generated/**`. It is a path heuristic — it does not inspect the emitted schema — so it trips on edits that provably cannot change the OpenAPI document, including a bare `import type { X } from "..."` path rewrite during a rename.

**Regenerating does not fix a true no-op.** An unchanged schema produces no diff under `packages/client/src/generated/**`, and the gate requires *either* a changed generated file *or* the sentinel. So for a genuine no-op the only exit is the sentinel:

```
[client-regen-not-needed]
```

It is matched by `git log "$BASE_SHA"..HEAD --format=%B | grep -qF`, so it must appear in a **commit message on the branch** (any commit), not the PR body. The workflow comment documents it as the intended escape hatch for exactly this false positive.

Adding it via a message-only `git commit --amend` keeps the tree hash identical, so the Depot attestation survives — see [[reference_message_only_amend_preserves_depot_attestation]]. Justify the claim in the message (paste the diff) so it stays auditable rather than a rubber stamp.

Hit on PR #2741, where `gateway/gateway/` → `gateway/worker-dispatch/` rewrote one `import type` line in `agent-config.ts` and `agent-history.ts`.

Both PRs are merged and the guardrail is live on main.

- **#2741** `refactor(server,agent-worker): structural pass…` → `5e087304`
- **#2742** `ci: add directory-structure gate` → `4904a4ae`

**What shipped**

| Surface | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| `manage_operations.ts` | 3,780 | 65-line facade + 5 handlers |
| `deployment-manager.ts` | 2,951 | 2,300 + 4 siblings |
| `tool-policy.ts` | 667 | 347 + `bash-command-parser.ts` |
| `gateway/gateway/index.ts` | repeated segment | `worker-dispatch/worker-gateway.ts` |

Plus a CI gate that mechanically rejects both shapes from returning.

**Three things worth your attention**

The rebase nearly reverted merged work. #2734 landed page-activation logic in `manage_operations.ts` mid-flight — the exact file being collapsed. I hand-ported it and verified 43/44 added lines verbatim (the 44th being the re-depthed import); its integration suite passes 10/10.

The reviewer caught a real gap in my own guardrail — it excluded the whole `client` package while claiming to exclude only generated output, silently leaving ~670 lines ungoverned. Fixed, and I mutation-tested the new fixture: restoring the exclusion fails exactly that test.

The `typecheck` red was the generated-client gate, not `tsc`. The sentinel was the only valid fix, and amending only the message preserved the tree hash, so the Depot attestation carried over.

**Confidence**

- *Refactor correctness* — **high (90)**. Independent AST comparison confirmed all 53 `manage_operations` and 11 `tool-policy` bodies preserved, 65/66 in `deployment-manager` (the exception being the deliberate `disableSystemdRunForSession()` delegation); 773 local tests pass; two 18-job Depot gates and full GitHub CI green.
- *Guardrail behavior* — **high (88)**. Verified in both directions on real trees and mutation-tested. Basis is direct execution, not inference.
- *Runtime behavior in prod* — **medium (70)**. This is import-graph and file-placement work with no logic change, and I did not boot the app and exercise flows end to end. Nothing here is prod-visible in the usual sense, so I did not set a rollout-verify wakeup.

**Suggested next actions**

1. Boot the app once and exercise a Behavior run plus a `manage_operations` execute, since "compiles + tests" is not the same as the real dispatch path.
2. Clear the 12 orphaned embedded-postgres instances (31/32 shm segments) — that ceiling has now produced two phantom test failures.
3. Consider the remaining large files a follow-up pass: I stopped at four, and the audit artifact lists the rest with the complexity-vs-size argument for each.
4. Decide whether the peer-session Depot contention needs a convention — it cost real wall-clock here and will recur.

input.description: Check for a peer session's running gate before dispatching Depot or re-running CI — newest dispatch cancels the older run, on Depot and on GitHub Actions alike.
input.content:
---
name: reference_check_for_a_peer_gate_before_dispatching
description: Check for a peer session's running gate before dispatching Depot or re-running CI — newest dispatch cancels the older run, on Depot and GitHub Actions alike.
metadata:
  type: reference
---

**Both** CI systems in this repo cancel the older run when a newer one is dispatched, so a careless dispatch destroys someone else's in-flight result:

- **Depot** serializes org-wide — see [[reference_depot_concurrency_policy_cancels_org_wide]].
- **GitHub Actions CI** has an auto-cancel concurrency group ("a newer main SHA contains every older main SHA"), scoped per ref.

Before `make pre-pr-remote` / `make pre-pr-remote-fast`, check:

```
pgrep -fl "make pre-pr-remote" | grep -v "grep\|eval\|snapshot"
```

A hit means another session (or another worktree) owns the slot. Wait for it rather than dispatching — chain it so the wait and the dispatch are one job, otherwise you check, find it free, and race the peer anyway:

```
while pgrep -f "make pre-pr-remote" >/dev/null; do sleep 25; done
make pre-pr-remote
```

Symptom of losing this race: your gate is killed seconds after starting with no output beyond your own echo. AGENTS.md line ~67 covers "never start a simultaneous **local** full gate" but says nothing about two sessions both dispatching **remotely**.

**`gh run rerun` counts as a dispatch.** Re-running an OLD commit's CI makes it the newest dispatch for that ref and cancels the run for the CURRENT HEAD. On 2026-08-13 this cancelled main's CI for `4904a4ae` because I re-ran `5e087304`'s to test a flake theory. To investigate an old commit's failure, reproduce locally instead; only ever `gh run rerun` the ref's current HEAD.

Related: [[feedback_check_for_a_peer_session_on_the_pr_queue]].

Never start a simultaneous local full gate, and check for a peer session's remote gate before dispatching (`pgrep -f "make pre-pr-remote"`) — Depot serializes org-wide, so a newer dispatch silently cancels the older run. Subset runs (`REMOTE_JOBS=…`) never attest.

- Never poll in the foreground (`sleep`/`until`/`while` loops, repeated `tail`). Run long waits in the background and act on the completion notification.

input.content:
# Agent playbook

Reasoning, incident history, and exact flags behind the rules in the repo-root `AGENTS.md`.

`AGENTS.md` is inlined into every agent session, so it carries the rules and nothing else. This file carries the *why*. Read the relevant section when a rule looks arbitrary, when you are about to argue yourself out of one, or when you need the full command.

Mechanical traps (build, SQL, testing, submodule, browser) live in `docs/GOTCHAS.md` instead.

## Workspace

**Explicit-path staging.** A commit is a snapshot of the index, not a diff of your intentions. A worktree that hosted earlier work still holds those files; `git add -A` commits the stale copies, which silently reverts already-merged PRs. Verify a "reverts merged work" review finding by diff direction against `origin/main` — never dismiss it as merge-base noise.

**One branch = one concern** means one concern, not one file. Split only for genuinely independent concerns or when the diff would be unreviewable.

## Data

**Request paths never aggregate history.** History only grows, so read-time aggregation cost grows with it while the answer stays bounded — the query gets slower every day for a result that does not change shape. Materialize the row or counter at write time and read it back by index. Run the one-time backfill in a migration, never per request.

**`events.id` is a stored-version id.** Connector resyncs supersede a row and allocate a new id for the same source item, so any identity or dedupe keyed on `events.id` breaks silently on the next resync.

**Organization rows.** Empty-looking orgs are frequently real human signups that have not been used yet. There is no bulk-delete that is safe, including "zero activity" filters.

## Runtime

**Dynamic-import exceptions.** Two call sites are grandfathered because they gate on the Node version before loading a large graph, and both must stay dependency-free until their checks pass:
- `packages/cli/bin/lobu.js` defers the existing CLI graph without duplicating it.
- `packages/server/src/server-entry.ts` puts an 842-byte gate in front of the 4.34 MB server graph (measured 2026-07-24).

**Fail closed on durable state.** The failure mode this prevents: an operation that may already have succeeded is retried as if nothing happened, or an error is read as "safe to skip" and a delivery is dropped. Treat ambiguity as failure and reconcile idempotently.

**Coordination design brake.** If a change needs a second lock, a second retry budget, or a prose argument for why it terminates, the check is in the wrong place. Re-derive where the decision belongs before adding mechanism.

## Evidence

**Red→fix→green.** Both outputs belong in the PR body. If you cannot reproduce the bug, that is a reportable dead end — a speculative fix costs more than the bug.

**Mutation checks.** A test that passes after you break the code proves nothing. Assert the old pattern exists, make a countable source change, confirm the focused test fails, then restore and rerun green.

**Absence needs `origin/main`.** A working-tree grep proves nothing about what exists — your tree is stale by definition. `git fetch -q origin && git grep <pattern> origin/main`; the fetch is load-bearing because `origin/main` itself goes stale.

**Never done off a typecheck.** Boot it, exercise every branch you touched, clean up test data you created. "It compiles" is a legitimate report only if you say that is all you ran.

## Gates

| Command | What it actually does |
|---|---|
| `make pre-pr-remote` | Full Linux CI graph on Depot against the **staged** tree; builds before checks that consume dist, which is what protects against a stale-dist false green. Fails closed on untracked/unstaged changes so the tree attestation survives the following commit. |
| `make pre-pr-remote-fast` | Broad interim confidence, remote. Never substitutes for the final gate. |
| `make pre-pr` | CPU-heavy local fallback for when Depot is unavailable. |
| `make review` | LLM verdict only. Runs no typecheck, knip, or tests — **not** proof CI will pass. |
| `make review-fix` | Unposted fixer pass. Edits the working tree; re-read files before trusting them. |
| `make ui-review` | Publishes UI proof; passes non-Owletto changes as not applicable. |

The macOS app lane stays on GitHub/Mac hardware. Subset runs (`make pre-pr-remote REMOTE_JOBS=unit`) rerun one lane but never attest. `make review` requires the matching full Depot tree attestation and refuses a surprise local build; only a documented Depot outage permits `REVIEW_ALLOW_LOCAL_BUILD=1 make review`.

**Depot serializes org-wide.** A newer dispatch silently cancels the older run, and `gh run rerun` counts as a dispatch — re-running an *old* commit's CI cancels the run for the current HEAD. Check `pgrep -f "make pre-pr-remote"` before dispatching, and chain the wait and the dispatch into one command so you do not check, find it free, and race a peer anyway. Several long-lived worktrees run their own gates concurrently, so this is common.

**`make review` skip rule.** Small safe-class diffs (docs, renames, generated, additive tests; under 100 lines) skip the cross-harness reviewer by default. `REVIEWER_MODE=full make review` forces the independent review; `REVIEWER_SHADOW=1` measures the skip rule instead of trusting it.

**UI proof.** `gh` cannot upload images inline. Capture before shots from the unmodified branch and after shots from the same booted app (auth recipe in `docs/BROWSER_TESTING.md`), base64-embed the PNGs into one self-contained HTML comparison page, publish it as a claude.ai artifact, and pass that URL as `ARTIFACT` to `make ui-review`. The gate records it on the exact merged Owletto PR, links it from the parent, and binds human approval to that parent-base and Owletto-pointer pair. No `ARTIFACT` means no proof and no pass.

## Post-merge rollout verification

For a prod-visible surface, set a self-rescheduling `ScheduleWakeup` (~1500s) that polls the deployed SHA and then runs:

```sh
MERGE_SHA=$(gh pr view <n> --json mergeCommit --jq .mergeCommit.oid)
git merge-base --is-ancestor "$MERGE_SHA" "$DEPLOYED_SHA"
```

Two ways this gate silently never opens:
- **Gating on the branch head instead of the squash commit.** A squash merge writes a new commit with no ancestry link to the branch, so the branch head exits 1 forever — PR #2280 has identical trees and still fails.
- **Reversing the argument order.** Merge commit first; reversed, it accepts a stale deploy.

Write the result back to memory when it lands.

## Session efficiency

- Exact local tests remain the fastest red-green loop; Depot owns CPU-heavy breadth. Never start a local full gate alongside a remote one.
- `make dev-remote` syncs tracked code to private Daytona compute, resumes or starts Lobu, and prints a signed preview URL. Commit first. Run `make dev-remote-pause` when finished, and keep it private — no hooks, public preview, or custom proxy.
- `gh pr checks <n> --required` plus a narrow `gh pr view --json` is the compact status read. `--json statusCheckRollup` measured 7520 bytes against 861 on PR 2280 — 8.7x larger and less legible.
- Delegated CLIs (OpenCode, Claude CLI) get polled at most once per 4.5 minutes, reading only output since the last cursor. Ask them to persist detailed evidence to files and return compact status, counts, and exit codes; never replay a full session or stream verbose diffs into the supervising context.
- Screenshots are the single largest context-bloat source. Prefer `get_page_text` / `read_page` / `javascript_tool`, and screenshot only when visual layout itself is under test.

content.text:
Confirmed: five rules are stated twice, in both **Hard invariants** and **Ship a change**. Here's the audit.

## Cut — these don't earn a permanent slot

**"Fix unused params by deleting them, not `_`-prefixing."** This is a linter's job. If it matters, it's a Biome rule; if Biome won't enforce it, it's too minor to spend a permanent line on. It's the only pure style nit in the file.

**"Skim `docs/GOTCHAS.md` for the surface you are touching"** — the *skim before you start* half. Untriggered "read this doc first" instructions get ignored, because nothing fires them. The second half — *grep it when something looks inexplicable* — is triggered and actionable. Keep that, drop the preamble.

**"Never `--json statusCheckRollup` — 8.7x larger."** A token micro-optimization sitting in the file that costs tokens on every session. It's already in the playbook with the measurement. The compact-read command is worth keeping; the anti-pattern footnote isn't.

## Dedupe — stated twice, so state it once

Five rules appear in both **Hard invariants** and **Ship a change**: `review-fix`, red→green, `ui-review`, explicit-path staging, `pre-pr-remote`. The procedure is the version people actually follow, step by step. My call: strip these from the invariants list and let the numbered procedure own them, leaving invariants for things that aren't a step in a sequence. That's roughly 5 dense bullets gone with zero rule loss.

## Relocate — real rules, wrong file

**"Fail closed on durable dispatch/delivery state"** and **"Coordination design brake."** Both are excellent and both are ~4 lines of abstract architecture prose. Ask honestly: has an agent ever *correctly applied* the coordination brake from this description alone, without already being deep in dispatch code? These belong in `packages/server/AGENTS.md`, next to `job-router` — where the rule already names the chokepoint. Every session pays for them; only dispatch work uses them.

**"Interactive browser drafts are page-activated, never tab-pushed."** Same argument, more so — it governs one feature. Belongs with the extension/connector package.

**"Mutation checks must prove the mutation landed."** Correct and important, but it only fires when you're mutation-testing, which is rare. → playbook.

That's ~12 lines of the always-loaded file moved to where they're actually read.

## Keep — and I'd argue for these

The ones I'd defend hardest all share a shape: **silent, expensive, and counterintuitive.**

- **Explicit-path staging.** Silently reverts merged PRs. Nothing else catches it.
- **`events.id` is not stable identity.** Breaks on the *next* resync, not this one.
- **Absence needs `origin/main`.** I nearly got this wrong myself today.
- **Never write to `~/Code/lobu`.** Corrupts other live sessions.
- **Multi-replica correctness.** Works perfectly in dev, fails in prod.
- **Workers never receive real credentials.** Security boundary.
- **Never done off a typecheck** and **show the diff, not a summary.** These two target the most common agent failure there is — claiming completion from weak evidence.
- **Behavior vs `watcher`.** The DB says `watcher`, so an agent gets it wrong by default. The prose saves a failed gate cycle.
- **Web-UI merge conflicts.** 1000+ lines lost, documented.

## The structural observation

Your three headings sort by *topic*, but the rules actually sort by *severity*. "Two writing agents must never share a worktree" sits under **Agent workflow**, yet it causes silent data loss — that's as hard an invariant as anything in the invariants list. Meanwhile "batch narrow fixes into one commit" is filed with it as an equal.

If you want the file to do real work, the split that matters is **"never do this, it's unrecoverable"** vs **"here's how to work efficiently."** An agent under pressure skims for the first kind and can safely skip the second. Right now both are interleaved at the same visual weight, which is why long rule files degrade — everything is bold, so nothing is.

## Net

Cut 3, dedupe 5, relocate 4. That's roughly another 25–30% off the auto-loaded file on top of the 30% already taken, with no rule deleted from the repo — only moved to where it fires.

Want me to apply this pass? I'd fold it into the same PR rather than merge the current version first, since the whole point is one considered edit to this file rather than three.
yes go do it. the anthropuc suggests deleting this file even over time because models get smarter and you are smarter compared to the model that generated that file so question everything

That premise is half right, and the half that's wrong matters.

A smarter model genuinely needs less *advice* — "write tests", "read before editing", style nits. But no amount of intelligence lets a model derive **contingent local facts** (`events.id` isn't stable identity; the DB says `watcher` but the product says `Behavior`; Depot serializes org-wide) or **authority boundaries** ("don't bulk-delete prod orgs", "get confirmation before changing the schema"). Those aren't reasoning gaps — they're knowledge and consent. A smarter model without them is *more* dangerous, not less, because it acts more confidently.

So my cutting rule: **delete advice, keep facts and permissions.** Let me re-read the current files first.

## Multi-replica correctness
- Production can run N>1 replicas. Before claiming a feature works, ask: “does this hold with 3 replicas?” Correctness must not depend on session affinity.
- Per-pod state (`SseManager`, event backlog, in-process worker map, deploy-lock cache) is pod-local. Cross-replica delivery must use Postgres (`thread_response` queue or equivalent).
- API/SSE terminal rows and interaction cards are owner-routed; non-owners requeue until the owning pod claims. Headless rows with no SSE client may be delivered by first claim.
- Streaming deltas/status are best-effort across pods today. Do not build correctness on cross-pod in-memory delivery.
- Exclusive transports such as Telegram polling run on exactly one replica via `connection_claims`; webhook transports must run on any replica.

## Connector operations and feed health
- Built-in connector definitions/catalog install in server; connector implementation details belong in `packages/connectors/AGENTS.md`.
- The active `connector_definitions` row is capability truth. Definitions may come from bundled source, organization-scoped `connector_versions`, or device manifests, so a grep under `packages/connectors` cannot prove an action is absent; inspect the active row and `operations.listAvailable`.
- Organization-scoped compiled code shadows the shared artifact for the active version. `refreshConnectorDefinitions` skips keys with no bundled source, but re-syncs every active key that does have bundled source and can reset its definition version/schema to bundled metadata; inspect the active definition after deploy instead of assuming an override survived.
- A data connection's `device_worker_id` is scrape affinity, not evidence that the browser is in front of the user. Connector-initiated browser actions currently inherit that pin. Until an interactive flow carries an explicit Chrome connection, a `completed` action proves execution on the selected extension, not that the user can see it; verify the resolved Chrome connection/worker before claiming delivery.
- Connector health scans `connections` + `feeds`; chat connections are not collector connections and should not trip zero-feed collector health rules.
- Feed hard auto-pause emits `feed.auto_paused` (Behavior signal + lifecycle event). Prefer a normal Behavior over new special-case agent subsystems.

<!-- Rules for agents (Claude, pi, codex); CLAUDE.md inlines this into every session. Keep it to facts an agent cannot derive and boundaries it must not cross. Reasoning and recipes go in docs/AGENT_PLAYBOOK.md, package specifics in the nearest package AGENTS.md. -->

## Repo map
- Bun workspace under `packages/*`; TS source in `src`, tests in `__tests__`.
- `core` types/utils · `plugin-api` plugin contracts · `plugin-host` plugin composition · `server` gateway + embedded runtime · `agent-worker` agent execution · `connectors` built-in connectors · `owletto` frontend submodule.
- Read the nearest package `AGENTS.md` before editing that package; grep `docs/GOTCHAS.md` when something looks inexplicable.

## Unrecoverable — never do these
- **Never write to `~/Code/lobu` directly.** Run `make task-setup NAME=<slug>` first, and never `git switch` in the main checkout — other sessions share it.
- **Stage by explicit path** (`git add -- <paths>`, never `-A`). A commit is a snapshot, so a stale file copy left by earlier work in the same worktree silently reverts merged PRs. After commit/rebase, `git diff --name-only origin/main...HEAD` must equal your intended file list; extras = stop.
- **`events` is append-only.** Never `DELETE FROM events`; tombstone or supersede instead.
- **Never bulk-delete prod `organization` rows**, including zero-activity ones — empty-looking orgs are usually real signups. Surface them one at a time for confirmation.
- **Never resolve merge conflicts in the GitHub web UI** — it has silently dropped 1000+ lines of feature work. Rebase locally against `origin/main`; submodule-pointer branches `git merge` instead (`docs/GOTCHAS.md`).
- **Two writing agents must never share a worktree** — they overwrite each other's uncommitted work. Every subagent with Edit/Write/Bash gets its own through `make task-setup`; only read-only agents share the parent.
- **Never add a table or change DB design, API surface, or SDK surface** without surfacing the proposal and receiving confirmation first.

## Facts you cannot derive
- **`events.id` is a stored-version id, not stable source identity.** A resync supersedes the row and mints a new id for the same source item, so cross-sync identity and dedupe must key on the connector's `origin_id` (scoped to its connection/source) or an explicit domain key.
- **Request paths never aggregate history.** No `GROUP BY`, `DISTINCT ON`, per-row `regexp_*`, or leading-wildcard `LIKE` over `events`, `agent_transcript_snapshot`, `session_calls`, … on a user-facing read path: history grows, the answer doesn't. Materialize at write time, read back by index, backfill in a migration. Bounded config tables (`connections`, `watchers`, `agent_users`) are fine.
- **Shared state must be Postgres-mediated.** An in-memory Map or singleton is invisible to other replicas — correct in dev, broken in prod.
- **Workers never receive real credentials** — placeholders or proxied access only. The exceptions are device-pinned connectors and short-lived provider-derived leases (`packages/server/AGENTS.md`); a durable stored credential is never one.
- **The product word is Behavior; `watcher` is DB/engine vocabulary.** `watcher` must not appear in MCP tool schemas, names, or descriptions, ClientSDK discovery metadata, or the connector-sdk public reaction contract — `make pre-pr-remote` fails on it. Internal identifiers and columns are fine.
- **`make review` is an LLM verdict, not CI.** It runs no typecheck, knip, or tests; passing it is not evidence CI will pass.
- **Depot serializes org-wide.** A newer dispatch silently cancels a peer session's running gate, and `gh run rerun` counts as a dispatch. Check `pgrep -f "make pre-pr-remote"` before dispatching.
- Default to static `import`; a new dynamic import needs measured justification plus a call-site rationale comment (two Node-version gates are grandfathered — playbook).

## Ship a change
1. `make task-setup NAME=<slug>` → work in `.claude/worktrees/<slug>/`.
2. Reproduce red → fix → prove green, and paste both outputs in the PR. Cannot reproduce = report the dead end; never ship a speculative fix.
3. Iterate on focused tests: `bun test <path>`, or `cd packages/server && bunx vitest run <path>` for vitest suites. `make pre-pr-remote-fast` gives interim breadth and never substitutes for the final gate.
4. `make review-fix` on the settled diff, then re-read what it touched. It runs BEFORE the first `make review` — never iterate `make review` as a find-fix loop, since each posted round costs a review + CI cycle.
5. Stage by explicit path, then `make pre-pr-remote`; it fails closed on unstaged or untracked changes. Reviewed workflow/action changes need `DEPOT_ALLOW_WORKFLOW_CHANGES=1`.
6. Commit, then confirm `git diff --name-only origin/main...HEAD` is exactly your intended file list.
7. `git push -u origin <branch>` → `gh pr create` (fill `.github/pull_request_template.md`; conventional-commit title).
8. `make review` **once** on the settled HEAD; it posts the required `pi-review` status.
9. `make ui-review`. Non-Owletto changes pass as not applicable; an Owletto pointer change needs exact hosted proof (`ARTIFACT=<url>`; capture recipe in `docs/BROWSER_TESTING.md`).
10. `gh pr merge <n> --squash --admin` once green — never `--admin` past a check that has not reported.
11. Prod-visible surface? Verify live after rollout: gate on the **squash commit**, not your branch head, keeping the argument order `git merge-base --is-ancestor "$MERGE_SHA" "$DEPLOYED_SHA"`. Record the result.

## How to work
- Do only what was asked. Delete ephemeral files you create; no new `*.md` unless asked.
- Run mandated gates automatically; never ask permission to run one.
- **Evidence, not assertion.** Never report done off a green typecheck — boot it, exercise every branch you touched, and clean up test data; if "compiles" is all you ran, say so. Show `git status` plus `git diff --stat <base>...HEAD`, including for a dispatched agent's work.
- **Absence needs `origin/main`:** `git fetch -q origin && git grep <pattern> origin/main`. A working-tree grep proves nothing, and the fetch is load-bearing.
- Deleting code needs structural evidence — a dangling import, a completed migration, a superseded implementation. Low prod usage is not evidence, and docs and help text are load-bearing.
- Fix the class, not the instance: on the first hit, grep every other occurrence and fix in one pass. A diff-scoped reviewer only ever finds the next one.
- One branch = one concern. Never `git stash`; use WIP commits.
- Prefer `bun`, never npm/yarn/pnpm. Before adding an env var, grep for the one already read, and do not rename existing vars unasked.
- Block only on irreversible or destructive actions and decisions genuinely the user's; otherwise take the recommended option and flag it in your summary.
- Never poll in the foreground — run long waits in the background and act on the notification. Poll delegated CLIs at most once every 4.5 minutes unless they finish or request input.
- Prefer DOM reads over screenshots, the top context-bloat source. The paired Owletto extension drives the user's real logged-in browser; CDP is not required (`docs/BROWSER_TESTING.md`).
- Slack link pasted → run `scripts/slack-thread-viewer.js "<link>"` first.
- `make dev-remote` runs a live app off your machine (commit first; `make dev-remote-pause` when finished).

- **Fail closed on durable dispatch/delivery state.** When a durable coordination or delivery operation fails, its caller must not reinterpret the error as proceed, deliver, or skip. Extension and server core carry no connector, Behavior, selector, or site-specific rules — connector/reaction code owns URL shapes and page interaction. Never auto-submit. +- **Fail closed on durable dispatch/delivery state.** When a durable coordination or delivery operation fails, its caller must not reinterpret the error as proceed, deliver, or skip. input.content:
## Summary

- Root `AGENTS.md` is inlined into every agent session via `CLAUDE.md`, so its length is a per-session context tax. It had grown to 16.3 KB / 74 lines, much of it rationale, incident history, and exact flags that an agent only needs when a rule looks arbitrary or it needs the full command. Cut to **7.6 KB / 53 lines (−53%)** by keeping only facts an agent cannot derive and boundaries it must not cross, restructured by severity: Repo map → Unrecoverable → Facts you cannot derive → Ship a change → How to work.
- The displaced material moves to a new `docs/AGENT_PLAYBOOK.md` (rationale, incident history, gate table, rollout verification, session efficiency) rather than being deleted; three architecture rules move to `packages/server/AGENTS.md`, which is where they apply. Nothing load-bearing was dropped — every cut was audited rule by rule.
- All seven package `AGENTS.md` files described the root gates as "`make pre-pr` + `make review`", which is wrong twice: `make pre-pr-remote` is the gate (`make pre-pr` is the local fallback), and `make review` runs no typecheck, knip, or tests. Fixed as a class; they now defer to the root doc.

## Test plan
- [x] Intended files staged explicitly, then `make pre-pr-remote` clean (full Linux CI graph on Depot; `make pre-pr` only as local fallback)
- [ ] Tests run: `make test-unit` / `make test-integration` / targeted `bun test <path>`
- [ ] Bug fix: red→fix→green outputs pasted below
- [ ] If bot behavior: ran `./scripts/test-bot.sh` or relevant eval

Documentation-only change; no runtime surface. `make pre-pr-remote` covers the referenced-path and vocabulary checks that do apply to these files.

## Notes

Rules cut as derivable-from-tooling rather than relocated: `_`-prefixing unused params, the `statusCheckRollup` payload anti-pattern, read-before-edit, batch-narrow-fixes, and doing repetitive multi-file edits inline. Five rules stated in both "Hard invariants" and "Ship a change" were deduped to one statement each.
